newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Crime wave gives Cyprus image a bashing.
newsitem.headline: Crime wave gives Cyprus image a bashing.

text.p: People can still walk a street at night without getting mugged, leave cars unlocked, sleep on the balcony and leave front doors open during the hot summer nights.
But they could get up one morning and find a mangled mass of metal instead of a car.

Car bombs exploding in the night, gunmen toting Kalashnikovs to ambush owners of seedy cabarets or gambling clubs and an explosion on Tuesday that nearly killed a judge and his young daughters have given the crime-free image of Cyprus a bashing.
"There is no doubt crime has gone beyond the control of the authorities," the mass-selling daily Philelephtheros said in an editorial on Wednesday.
"Crime has reached the point of audacity where it looks at nothing."

Although it has not had an impact on bookings yet, unsolved crimes among underworld figures, who everyone seems to have heard of, could tarnish the image of the holiday island that attracts some two million tourists a year.
In Limassol, a bustling port city on the island's southern coast, criminal gangs are believed to be waging a turf war over brothels and extortion rackets.

Police suspect that in some cases they use foreigners, mainly eastern Europeans and Russians, to do the dirty work. Last week two Russians were detained on suspicion of planting a bomb under the car of a Nicosia businessman in August. They said they were paid by a Greek Cypriot, who so far has not been arrested.

But moving more into mainstream society, a Limassol judge and his five-year-old daughters narrowly escaped a car bomb attack on Tuesday. The judge tried traffic offences and civil cases in Limassol district court.
Greek Cypriots were outraged by the ruthlessness of the attack on the judge and his triplet daughters whom he was about to take to school.
"We are still trying to establish a motive," police spokesman Glafcos Xenos told Reuters. The bombing was similar to one that killed a pub owner in southeastern Cyprus in early September.
Last year police solved 71 percent of serious crimes reported but they admit to having little success with bombings.
"It is non-existent," one senior police source told Reuters. "That is because of the nature of the crime. It is not as though we are incompetent."
Instead, police blame the public for refusing to cooperate and on loopholes in laws on detaining suspects. But the police can hardly be surprised at the public's reluctance to trust them.

Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides himself earlier this year said police officers were involved in at least one murder and one murder attempt last year. That case is still under review at the attorney-general's office.
